Choose one release proof boundary

decision

Three approaches reduce duplicate release work. Only one preserves a literal chain from verification to publication.

The decision

Choose the smallest release architecture that proves the exact candidate once, then passes that same artifact to packaging and upload. This is illustrative content; replace every claim with evidence from the real system.

Non-negotiable. A successful source build is not proof of a separately reconstructed upload candidate.

Three viable approaches

Keep separate gates

Each release stage builds its own artifact. Familiar, but no single receipt identifies what shipped.

best for: disposable development builds

Freeze one candidate

Recommended. Build once, verify the immutable candidate, then package and upload that exact path.

best for: releases that need auditable proof

Trust remote CI

Publish after external checks report green. Simple locally, but the remote result still needs an artifact identity contract.

best for: mature artifact-producing CI

Shared criteria expose the real tradeoff

CriterionSeparate gatesFrozen candidateRemote CI
Candidate identityChanges by stageStable end to endDepends on CI contract
Duplicate workHighLowLow locally
Failure receiptFragmentedOne local chainSplit across systems
Operational changeNoneContainedBroad

The cost worth accepting

The frozen candidate approach adds explicit artifact ownership to the release path. That is a real change, but it is smaller than importing a new CI architecture and directly closes the proof gap.

Recommendation

Freeze one candidate and make every later stage consume it. Record the candidate identifier, focused verification results, and publication receipt in one release summary.

Do not widen this work into a build-system rewrite; preserve the existing build command and change only artifact handoff.
